lessons.title: Pre-Money, Post-Money and the Basic Dilution Formula

children.text: A Series A term sheet lands in Meera's inbox: ₹6.25 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹18.75 crore. Two numbers, one line, and every founder reads it the same way at first, which is as a compliment. The useful question is different. What percentage of TiffinBox does Meera own on the morning after this closes, and was there a better version of the same deal?

body.text: Dilution is not a mystery and it is not decided by the valuation alone. Your dilution in any round is simply the money raised divided by the post-money valuation. Everything else is negotiation around those two numbers.

markDefs.definition: The agreed value of the company immediately before new investment money is added. Adding the investment to it gives the post-money valuation.

children.text: is what the company is worth before the cheque. Add the cheque and you get the post-money valuation. The investor's share of the company is their cheque divided by that post-money number. There is no fourth number hiding anywhere.

body.caption: The only two formulas you need to read a term sheet's headline

children.text: For TiffinBox: ₹18.75 crore plus ₹6.25 crore gives a post-money valuation of ₹25 crore. The investor's stake is ₹6.25 crore ÷ ₹25 crore, which is 25%. That single percentage is the dilution the whole existing cap table shares between them.

body.label: Price per share
body.context: Pre-money ÷ pre-round fully diluted shares = ₹18,75,00,000 ÷ 18,750 = ₹10,000. Every new share in this round is issued at that price, and the investor's ₹6.25 crore buys 6,250 of them.

content.caption: From rupees to shares, and from old percentage to new

children.text: TiffinBox had 18,750 fully diluted shares after the seed round. Price per share = ₹18,75,00,000 ÷ 18,750 = ₹10,000. New shares = ₹6,25,00,000 ÷ ₹10,000 = 6,250. Total after the round = 18,750 + 6,250 = 25,000 shares. Investor check: 6,250 ÷ 25,000 = 25.00%.

Meera held 32.00% before the round. Her new stake is 32.00% × (1 - 0.25) = 24.00%. Cross-check with share counts: 6,000 ÷ 25,000 = 24.00%. Both routes always agree, which makes the multiplier a fast way to sanity-check any term sheet in your head.

body.caption: TiffinBox before and after the Series A (fully diluted)

children.text: Every existing holder lost exactly one quarter of their previous percentage. That is what a 25% round does: it takes a quarter of everyone, in proportion. Nobody is singled out, which is why arguments about dilution are really arguments about the two headline numbers.

body.text: Always ask whether a quoted valuation is pre-money or post-money. "We will put in ₹4 crore at ₹20 crore" means 16.67% if that ₹20 crore is pre-money (4 ÷ 24), and 20% if it is post-money (4 ÷ 20). That is 3.33 percentage points of your company riding on one unasked question. Get it written into the term sheet in words, not just numbers.

children.text: Valuation Is Only Half the Negotiation

Founders fixate on valuation because it is the number that gets repeated in press coverage. Dilution is driven by the ratio of the two numbers, so a larger cheque at a proportionally higher valuation costs you nothing extra. Compare three versions of the same TiffinBox round.

body.caption: Three versions of the same round

cells: A: the term sheet on the table
C: more money, proportionally higher valuation

children.text: Version C raises 60% more money than version A for exactly the same dilution, because the valuation rose in step with the cheque. That is the trade founders should be hunting for, rather than chasing a headline valuation with a small cheque attached that buys twelve months of runway.

columns.label: The highest valuation you can get
points: Less dilution today and a better headline
Sets a high bar you must grow into before the next round

Often comes with tougher terms elsewhere in the document

columns.label: Enough money to reach the next milestone

body.text: One thing quietly breaks the clean arithmetic above: the ESOP pool. Most term sheets require the pool to be topped up before the round, out of the pre-money valuation, which means the existing shareholders absorb it and the founders take more than the headline dilution. The next lesson takes that apart in detail, because it is where founders lose the most ground without noticing.

body.title: Read the term sheet
body.prompt: A Kolkata logistics startup is offered ₹7.5 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹30 crore. What percentage of the company will the new investor own immediately after the round, ignoring any ESOP pool change?
body.explanation: Post-money = ₹30 crore + ₹7.5 crore = ₹37.5 crore. Investor share = 7.5 ÷ 37.5 = 20%. Every existing holder keeps 80% of whatever percentage they held before.

body.title: Name the denominator
body.textWithBlank: An investor's percentage is their investment divided by the ___-money valuation.
body.explanation: Dividing by the pre-money valuation overstates the investor's stake and understates what you keep. Post-money is pre-money plus the investment.

body.title: Same money, different meaning
body.question: An investor says: "We will invest ₹5 crore at ₹20 crore." Which reading is worse for the founders, and by how much?
options: The ₹20 crore is pre-money, which gives the investor 25%
The ₹20 crore is post-money, which gives the investor 25%, four percentage points more than the 20% they would get on a pre-money reading
Both readings give the investor exactly the same stake
The ₹20 crore is post-money, which gives the investor 20%
body.explanation: On a post-money reading the investor gets 5 ÷ 20 = 25%. On a pre-money reading, post-money is ₹25 crore and the investor gets 5 ÷ 25 = 20%. The post-money reading is worse for founders by four percentage points, which is why the term sheet must say which one it means.

body.title: Two term sheets, one decision
body.scenario: You run a Bengaluru B2B SaaS company burning ₹40 lakh a month, with eight months of cash left. You hold 45% fully diluted. Term sheet A: ₹8 crore at ₹32 crore pre-money, from a fund you like, closing in six weeks. Term sheet B: ₹12 crore at ₹36 crore pre-money, from a fund that wants a board seat and monthly reporting, closing in ten weeks. Assume no ESOP pool change in either.
body.prompt: Work out the dilution and your stake under each, then decide which you would take and why.
body.modelAnswer:
The arithmetic:
Term sheet A: post-money = ₹32 crore + ₹8 crore = ₹40 crore. Dilution = 8 ÷ 40 = 20%. Your stake = 45% × 0.80 = 36.00%. Runway added = ₹8 crore ÷ ₹40 lakh = 20 months.
Term sheet B: post-money = ₹36 crore + ₹12 crore = ₹48 crore. Dilution = 12 ÷ 48 = 25%. Your stake = 45% × 0.75 = 33.75%. Runway added = ₹12 crore ÷ ₹40 lakh = 30 months.

The trade: B costs you 2.25 percentage points more today and buys ten extra months of runway, at a valuation that is 12.5% higher. B also comes with a board seat and reporting obligations, and closes four weeks later, which matters when you have eight months of cash.

How to decide:
1. What does the next valuation step need? If reaching a Series B story takes 24 months of building, A leaves you raising with four months of cash left, which is the weakest position a founder can be in.
2. Price the extra 2.25 points against that risk. Raising from weakness usually costs far more than 2.25 points.
3. Timing risk: ten weeks to close with eight months of runway is acceptable, but negotiate a signing deadline and check whether the fund has closed deals on schedule before.
4. The board seat is not automatically a cost. An engaged investor director can be useful. What matters is the list of reserved matters attached, which Chapter 4 covers.

A reasonable answer: take B if your plan genuinely needs more than 20 months, and use A's existence as leverage to negotiate B's governance terms. Take A if you are close to profitability and the extra cash would only fund experiments you are not ready to run.

body.title: Before you sign the headline numbers
steps: Confirm in writing whether the valuation is pre-money or post-money.
Calculate the investor's percentage as investment divided by post-money.
Multiply your current fully diluted stake by (1 minus the investor's percentage) to get your new stake.
Ask what pre-round share count the price per share is based on, and whether it includes the full ESOP pool and all convertibles.
Divide the money raised by your monthly burn to convert the round into months of runway.
Ask what milestones the next round will require, and whether this cheque funds them.
Test a bigger cheque at a proportionally higher valuation before assuming the offered structure is fixed.

cards.definition: The agreed value of the company immediately before the new investment is added.
Pre-money valuation plus the money invested in the round.
Pre-money valuation divided by the pre-round fully diluted share count.
Investment divided by post-money valuation. The proportion of the company transferred to the new investor.
One minus the round dilution. Multiply your old percentage by it to get your new one.
Cash available divided by monthly net burn, expressed in months.

points: Post-money valuation is pre-money plus the investment, and the investor's stake is the investment divided by post-money.
Every existing holder is diluted by the same proportion, so a 25% round leaves everyone with 75% of what they had.
Price per share is pre-money divided by the pre-round fully diluted share count. Ask what went into that share count.
A bigger cheque at a proportionally higher valuation costs no extra dilution, so negotiate the pair of numbers, not just the valuation.
Always confirm whether a quoted valuation is pre-money or post-money. On a ₹5 crore cheque at ₹20 crore, the difference is four percentage points.
Convert every offer into months of runway and ask whether that funds the milestones the next round will demand.
An ESOP top-up taken out of the pre-money valuation breaks the clean arithmetic, which is the subject of the next lesson.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other startups described are fictional, and all valuations, share counts and prices are illustrative. Real rounds involve pricing rules, valuation reports and regulatory requirements that depend on the investor and the structure. Consult a qualified chartered accountant, company secretary or lawyer before agreeing or closing a fundraise.
